citation.description: test_container_recreate_orphan_is_reclaimed: seeds a stamp with OLD_CONTAINER hostname and OLD_NS, then poses as NEW_CONTAINER/NEW_NS with same boot_id, calls acquire() and asserts it succeeds promptly. _mkdir_lock_is_stale uses _host_identity() (boot_id-based) at lock.py:347, so same boot_id => same host => cross-namespace reclaim via fcntl_held=True at lock.py:354.

criteria.criterion: A lock orphaned by a dead process on the SAME host is reclaimable even when the recorded hostname differs because the process ran in a since-recreated container; verified by a test that simulates a changed gethostname() with a dead pid.

citation.description: test_live_owner_in_same_namespace_is_still_never_reclaimed (lines 99-108) asserts _mkdir_lock_is_stale returns False for a live pid even with fcntl_held=True. test_foreign_host_is_still_never_reclaimed (lines 111-128) asserts a different boot_id is never reclaimed. lock.py:347 unconditionally returns False for different host identity. Pre-existing yaw-gravel-linen tests in test_lock_stale_reclaim.py (test_acquire_does_not_reclaim_live_owner, test_acquire_does_not_reclaim_foreign_host_owner) also cover this.

criteria.criterion: A lock owned by a LIVE process is still never reclaimed, and a genuinely foreign-host lock is still not reclaimed on the strength of hostname alone; verified by tests (no regression of bug yaw-gravel-linen).

citation.description: LockTimeout is caught and logged as logger.warning (not silently swallowed). The container-recreate incident class is now provable via boot_id + fcntl proof, so it does not stall at all. The remaining unprovable foreign-host case surfaces as a WARNING log rather than a silent 60s stall.

criteria.criterion: An unprovable lock does not block indefinitely: either an age ceiling applies or the failure is surfaced rather than silently swallowed into a 60s stall.
